ref: DAR — Daniel ch. 7: The Four Beasts
title: The Four Beasts
voicePrompt: In your own words, walk through Smith's argument that the four beasts of Daniel 7 cover the same ground as the great image of chapter 2 — Babylon, Medo-Persia, Grecia, and Rome — and explain how the little horn that rises among Rome's ten divisions identifies the papacy, including its war on the saints and the 1260-year period.

questions.stem: According to the chapter, how do we know the four beasts are symbols of kingdoms rather than merely individual kings?
options: The angel's explanation in verse 23 says the fourth beast 'shall be the fourth kingdom upon the earth'
Daniel personally counted four crowns on each beast
Each beast was named after a known monarch of the ancient world
The beasts all rose from the sea at the same moment
questions.explanation: Smith points out that although verse 17 calls them 'four kings,' the angel in verse 23 says 'The fourth beast shall be the fourth kingdom upon the earth,' and verse 18 adds that 'the saints shall take the kingdom' — showing kingdoms, not mere individuals, are intended.

questions.stem: How does the chapter interpret the symbolic 'winds' striving upon the 'great sea'?
options: Winds are angels and the sea is the abyss
Winds denote strife, political commotion, and war, while the sea (waters) denotes peoples, nations, and tongues
Winds are false doctrines and the sea is the church
Winds represent the four gospels and the sea represents the world
questions.explanation: Smith says winds 'denote strife, political commotion, and war' (citing Jeremiah 25), and that the Bible definition of sea or waters as a symbol is 'peoples, and nations, and tongues' (citing Revelation 17:15).

questions.stem: What does the chapter say the four beasts represent, and why is this vision given when chapter 2's image already covered the same ground?
options: Four future kingdoms not yet arisen; the image was about the past only
Four religious systems; the image was about politics only
The same four kingdoms as the great image (Babylon onward); the ground is repeated so additional characteristics and features can be brought out — 'line upon line'
Four empires entirely different from the image, given to correct an earlier error
questions.explanation: Smith argues the first beast denotes Babylon (the head of gold) and the rest the succeeding kingdoms shown by the image; the ground is 'passed over again and again that additional characteristics may be brought out... It is thus that we have line upon line,' showing the kingdoms' true character as wild, ravenous beasts.

questions.stem: How does the chapter explain the leopard's four wings and four heads?
options: Four wings show Grecia's unparalleled speed of conquest, and four heads the empire's division among Alexander's four generals
Four wings show the four winds of heaven, and four heads the four provinces of Babylon
Four wings represent the Medes, Persians, Greeks, and Romans, and four heads four cities
Four wings and four heads both represent the four divisions of the Roman empire
questions.explanation: Smith says the four wings denote 'unparalleled celerity of movement' true of Grecia under Alexander, and that the four heads were the division of the empire among his four leading generals — Cassander, Lysimachus, Ptolemy, and Seleucus.

questions.stem: What does the chapter identify the 'little horn' as, and which three horns were plucked up before it?
options: Pagan Rome; the Greeks, Lombards, and Franks
The papacy; the Heruli, the Vandals, and the Ostrogoths
Napoleon's empire; the Huns, Suevi, and Burgundians
The Eastern Roman Empire; the Visigoths, Anglo-Saxons, and Lombards
questions.explanation: Smith identifies the little horn as the papacy and states the three horns plucked up were the Heruli (A.D. 493), the Vandals (534), and the Ostrogoths (538), all Arian powers opposed to papal supremacy. (He rejects Mede's and Newton's lists of Greeks/Lombards/Franks and Exarchate/Lombards/Senate.)

questions.stem: How does the chapter interpret the scene of the Ancient of days, the thrones, and the opened books in verses 9-10?
options: The second advent of Christ to the earth to destroy the wicked
The casting down of earthly thrones at the last day
The opening of an investigative judgment in the heavenly sanctuary, where thrones are 'set up' (not 'cast down') and cases are examined
A symbolic picture of the millennium already in progress on earth
questions.explanation: Smith argues the word translated 'cast down' actually means 'to set up' or 'place,' so the thrones of judgment are set up in God's court on high. The opened books mark an investigative judgment — the closing of Christ's high-priestly ministry — determining beforehand who will receive eternal life.

questions.stem: How does the chapter calculate the 'time and times and the dividing of time' and apply it historically?
options: Three and a half literal years, fulfilled during a single papal reign
1260 literal days during which Rome was besieged
Three and a half symbolic years = 1260 prophetic days = 1260 years, from A.D. 538 to 1798, when Berthier took the pope prisoner
2300 years ending in 1844, marking the cleansing of the sanctuary
questions.explanation: Smith reckons a time = 1 year, times = 2 years, dividing of time = half a year, totaling 3.5 years or 1260 prophetic days; applying the day-for-a-year rule yields 1260 years. He dates this from A.D. 538 (Ostrogoths driven from Rome) to 1798, when Berthier entered Rome and took the pope prisoner: 538 + 1260 = 1798.

questions.stem: According to the chapter, how do verses 11-12 refute the ideas of a pre-advent millennium of gospel triumph or probation after Christ comes?
options: Because the fourth beast is converted to righteousness before the end
Because the fourth beast continues unchanged until it is destroyed (given to the burning flame), and unlike the earlier beasts its life is not prolonged after its dominion is gone
Because the saints reign on earth for a thousand years before the judgment sits
Because the little horn repents and joins the saints at the last day
questions.explanation: Smith argues the fourth beast keeps its character and the little horn its blasphemies until the beast is given to the flame — its destruction, not conversion. And unlike the earlier kingdoms whose lives were prolonged after losing dominion, the fourth beast ends in the lake of fire with no existence beyond, so there is no probation or mixed millennium after the Lord comes.
